Chapter 7: The Sacredness of Time—Mindfulness, Moderation, and the Value of Each Moment
Time has this quiet way of slipping by, doesn’t it? Most of the time, we barely notice it’s gone until we look back and realize how much has changed.
The Sunan Ibn Majah brings us back again and again to a simple truth: every moment is a gift. And the way we spend our days? It doesn’t just shape our own lives—it’s woven into the lives of everyone around us.
There’s a story I want to share—it’s about a craftsman, always busy, always feeling like he was just one step behind. His days were a blur, rushing from one task to the next. But then, one evening, he heard a teaching: the Prophet advised his companions to be mindful of their time, to avoid wastefulness, and to seek balance in everything.
That night, something shifted. The craftsman started to notice the little things—sharing a meal with his family, lending a hand to a neighbor, even just taking a few deep breaths before starting work. Slowly, his days felt less frantic. Life became a little more meaningful.
The hadith encourage us to live with intention. To avoid excess. To look for moderation in our work, our rest, and even in how we play. There’s a gentle, quiet wisdom in the Prophet’s approach to daily life—he never rushed, never wasted a moment, and always remained present.
It’s so easy to think that only the big achievements matter. But these teachings remind us—the ordinary moments, like greeting a friend, tending a garden, or listening to a child—those are just as sacred.
Mindfulness—what the tradition calls muraqabah—weaves through these lessons. It’s really about being aware: of your thoughts, your actions, and the needs of those around you. There’s another story, this time of a woman who felt overwhelmed by all her responsibilities. She decided to set aside just a few minutes each day for quiet reflection. That small habit brought her clarity and peace, helping her meet each challenge with more patience and grace.
The Prophet’s teachings also warn us about something we all struggle with: procrastination and regret. There’s a tale of a man who always said he’d do his good deeds “tomorrow.” But when an opportunity slipped away, he realized that lost time can’t be reclaimed. That lesson stuck with him—it made him act with more urgency and care.
In a world that’s always rushing and full of distractions, these hadith offer a gentle reminder: slow down. Pay attention. Cherish the moments that make up your life.
The Sunan Ibn Majah brings together these teachings to invite us to live each day with purpose, with gratitude, and with a sense of wonder for every single moment we’re given.
